preamble: Fortition of the voiceless dental fricative [θ] to the affricate [ts] is a rare change with no secure textbook case. The only candidate is Sardinian: the reflex of Latin -ti̯-/-ci̯- is [θ] in conservative Nuorese (e.g. Bitti) and [ts] (spelled tz) in much of the rest of the island. Following Meyer-Lübke and Wagner, medieval <th> is read as [θ] and the modern [ts] as a later development, but Swanenvleugel (2025) argues that an original affricate value ([tθ] or [ts]) is more plausible, which would make Nuorese [θ] the innovation. The direction of change is therefore contested.

examples.from: Latin puteus; Old Sardinian <th> (interpreted as [θ]); Nuorese púθθu 'well'
examples.note: Latin -ti̯- gives Nuorese [θ] versus [ts] elsewhere (Logudorese also has [t], as in púttu). The reading [θ] > [ts] follows Wagner (1941). Swanenvleugel (2025) prefers an original affricate value, which would make this cell the reverse of what actually happened.

sources: Swanenvleugel, C. (2025). The pre-Roman elements of the Sardinian lexicon. PhD dissertation, Leiden University. https://hdl.handle.net/1887/4180290
Wagner, M. L. (1941). Historische Lautlehre des Sardischen. Halle: Niemeyer.
